results.blind_working: Temperature does not depend on the amount of matter, so it is intensive. Volume, enthalpy and mass all scale with amount, so they are extensive.
Density, temperature and molar heat capacity are intensive. Gibbs energy, entropy and heat capacity all scale with amount, so option 4 contains only extensive properties.
Density and temperature are intensive, so they stay ρ and T. Heat capacity is extensive, so it halves to C/2.
Density = mass/volume (III). Molar heat capacity = C/n (IV). Molar volume = V/n (I). Heat capacity is extensive and is shared between the halves (II).

A is true: a ratio of extensives (e.g., mass/volume) is intensive. B is true. C is false because E° is intensive. D is true. E is false because surface tension and viscosity are intensive. So A, B and D.
Enthalpy, entropy and Gibbs energy are state functions. Work depends on the path taken, so it is a path function.
Over a complete cycle, every state function returns to its initial value, so ΔU, ΔH and ΔG are all zero. Heat q is a path function, so it need not be zero.
Path 1: q = +50 J and w = -20 J, so ΔU = 50 - 20 = 30 J. ΔU is the same for path 2, so w = ΔU - q = 30 - 40 = -10 J.
For an ideal gas, U depends only on T, so ΔU = 0 in an isothermal process and A is true. In an isothermal process heat is exchanged (q = -w), so R describes an adiabatic process and is false.
Entropy is a state function, so ΔS = 0 over a cycle, while q and w can be non-zero; Statement I is correct. q + w = ΔU, which is a state function and path-independent; Statement II is incorrect.
Free expansion: q, w, ΔU and ΔT all zero (IV). Reversible isothermal: ΔU = 0, q = −w (III). Adiabatic: q = 0, ΔU = w and the gas cools (I). Rigid vessel: w = 0, ΔU = q_V (II).

A is true. B is false: ΔH = q_p, not q_V. C is the intended true statement, since Δn_g = 0 makes ΔH ≈ ΔU. D is false: an ideal gas cools in adiabatic expansion. E is true: q = nRT ln10 = 2 × 8.314 × 300 × 2.303 ≈ 11.5 kJ.
For a monoatomic gas Cp = 5/2 R. q = nCpΔT = 2 × 2.5 × 8.314 × 50 = 2078.5 J ≈ 2.08 kJ
For a diatomic gas Cv = 5/2 R. ΔU = nCvΔT = 3 × (5/2)R × 20 = 150R, regardless of the process.

A is true: the coffee-cup calorimeter works at constant pressure (q = ΔH), the bomb calorimeter at constant volume (q = ΔU). R is true: Cp − Cv = R. R does not explain A; A follows from the constant P vs constant V conditions.
I is false: for an ideal gas, ΔU = nCvΔT holds for any process. II is true: Cp = 7/2 R, so q = 1 × 3.5R × 10 = 35R.
C + 1/2 O2 -> CO: subtract the CO combustion equation from the graphite combustion equation. ΔHf(CO) = -393.5 - (-283.0) = -110.5 kJ/mol
Subtract the SO2 equation from the SO3 equation: ΔH = -396 - (-297) = -99 kJ
A: reversing changes the sign of ΔH (III). B: multiplying by 3 multiplies ΔH by 3 (IV). C: adding equations sums the ΔH values (I). D: Born-Haber cycle gives lattice enthalpy (II).

A true: enthalpy is a state function. B false: reversing changes the sign of ΔH. C true: physical states must match. D true: e.g. ΔHf of CO cannot be measured directly. E false: total ΔH is independent of the path. Correct set is A, C, D.

By convention, ΔfH° = 0 only for an element in its most stable standard state. Graphite, O2(g) and Br2(l) are the reference forms. Diamond is not the reference form of carbon, so its ΔfH° (about +1.9 kJ/mol) is not zero.
ΔrH = Σ(bonds broken) − Σ(bonds formed) = (436 + 242) − 2(431) = 678 − 862 = −184 kJ.
Atomizing CH4 breaks four C-H bonds, so the average C-H bond enthalpy = 1664/4 = 416 kJ/mol.
ΔsolH = ΔlatticeH + ΔhydH. For NH4Cl the lattice enthalpy outweighs the magnitude of the hydration enthalpy, so ΔsolH is positive. Dissolution is therefore endothermic, and R correctly explains A.
Statement I is false because hydration enthalpy is negative. Statement II is false because ΔsubH = ΔfusH + ΔvapH, so ΔsubH is greater than ΔvapH.
When liquid water freezes to ice, its molecules become more ordered, so the entropy of the system decreases. Melting, evaporation and dissolution all increase disorder.
ΔS_fus = ΔH_fus/T = 6000 J/mol ÷ 273 K ≈ 22.0 J K^-1 mol^-1. The value is positive because fusion absorbs heat.
For isothermal expansion, ΔS = nR ln(V2/V1) = 8.314 × ln 10 = 8.314 × 2.303 ≈ 19.15 J/K. It is positive because the gas expands.

A (free expansion): ΔS_sys = nR ln(V2/V1) and ΔS_surr = 0, so III. B (reversible adiabatic): isentropic, so I. C (phase change at boiling point): ΔS = ΔH/T, so IV. D (spontaneous process): ΔS_univ > 0, so II.

A is false; not every exothermic process is spontaneous. B is true; melting of ice above 273 K is entropy-driven. C is true; at equilibrium ΔS_univ = 0. D is false; since ΔS = q/T, a given heat gives a smaller entropy increase at higher T. E is true; entropy is a state function. Correct set: B, C, E.
ΔG = ΔH − TΔS. With ΔH > 0 and ΔS > 0, ΔG becomes negative only when TΔS > ΔH, i.e. T > ΔH/ΔS.
Crossover T = ΔH/ΔS = 180000/150 = 1200 K. Since ΔS > 0, ΔG < 0 above 1200 K.
A is true: thermodynamic spontaneity says nothing about rate, which is a kinetic matter. R is a true fact about −ΔG being the maximum non-pV work, but it does not explain rate.

I: at constant T and P, ΔS_total = ΔS_sys − ΔH/T, so ΔG = −TΔS_total; I is correct. II: at 300 K, ΔG = −120 + 90 = −30 kJ/mol (negative); at 500 K, ΔG = −120 + 150 = +30 kJ/mol (positive); II is correct.
From ΔG° = −RT ln K, a positive ΔG° means ln K < 0. So K < 1 and reactants are favoured.
A: ΔG° < 0 gives K > 1 (III). B: ΔG° = 0 gives K = 1 (I). C: at equilibrium ΔG = 0 and Q = K (IV). D: a tenfold rise in K lowers ΔG° by 2.303RT ≈ 5.7 kJ/mol (II).

A is true: ΔG = 0 at equilibrium, but ΔG° is generally nonzero. B is true: equal concentrations give K = 1, so ΔG° = 0 and ΔS° = ΔH°/T. C is true: ΔG = RT ln(Q/K), which is negative when Q < K. D is false: K = 10⁻³ gives ΔG° = +17.1 kJ/mol, not −17.1.
